header_title: Why Heavy Things Don't Fall Faster
tagline: Force and inertia cancel in free fall
question_text: Why do a heavy ball and a light ball land together?
audio_script: Push an empty shopping cart. It rolls away easily. Now load it with bricks and push with the same effort. It crawls. Nothing about your push changed. The cart's mass changed, and with it the cart's response to your push. This is Newton's second law: net force equals mass times acceleration. Rearrange it. Acceleration equals force divided by mass. The acceleration is what you see. The force is what you do. The mass is what the object resists with. Now the strange part. Drop a heavy ball and a light ball from the same height. Which lands first? Aristotle said the heavy one. Almost everyone's intuition agrees. But they land together. Why? The heavy ball feels a bigger gravitational pull: twice the mass, twice the weight. But twice the mass also means twice the inertia, twice the resistance to being moved. The two effects cancel exactly. The acceleration comes out the same. Galileo's famous experiment was shocking not because objects fall, but because the thing that should have made the heavy one fall faster is exactly the thing that makes it harder to move at all. Force and inertia are two sides of one coin. This is why, when the only force is gravity, mass drops out of the equation entirely. In a vacuum, a hammer and a feather fall side by side. On Earth the feather loses because air pushes back on it, and that push depends on shape, not on mass. Strip the air away, and the difference disappears. The second law works in every direction, independently. Write it once for x, once for y, once for z. This is why a thrown ball keeps moving sideways at the same speed while it falls. The horizontal motion does not know the vertical motion exists. They do not interfere. That single fact is the entire logic of projectile motion.

header_title: The Moon Is Falling
tagline: It has been falling for four billion years
question_text: Why does the Moon keep missing the Earth?
audio_script: Newton's apple is the most famous fruit in physics. But the apple is only half the story. Newton's real question was about the Moon. Why does the Moon go around the Earth instead of falling onto it? Here is the answer he found. The Moon is falling. It has been falling for four and a half billion years. It just keeps missing. Imagine throwing a ball horizontally from a very tall tower. Throw it gently, and it lands a little way off. Throw it harder, and it lands farther. Throw it hard enough, and something strange happens. The Earth curves away beneath it as fast as the ball falls toward it. The ball is falling the whole time, but the ground is also dropping away. It never lands. That is an orbit. The Moon is doing exactly this. Gravity pulls it toward Earth, constantly, without pause. But the Moon has just the right sideways speed, so instead of crashing, it curves around. And there is a beautiful relationship hiding in this. Set the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force needed to keep the Moon on its circle. The orbital speed comes out to v equals the square root of G M over r. It depends only on the central mass and the radius. Not on the Moon's mass. Not on what the Moon is made of. A tiny satellite and a giant moon at the same radius orbit at the same speed. Kepler noticed this from the data long before Newton explained it: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the radius. In Newton's hands, that becomes a statement about gravity itself. An inverse-square law that reaches across the solar system. Everything in space is a balance between falling, and moving sideways fast enough to keep missing.

header_title: The Universe Keeps Books
tagline: Two skaters push off and never meet again
question_text: Where does the motion come from when two skaters push apart?
audio_script: Two ice skaters stand at rest, facing each other, hands touching. They push. Immediately they move apart, one gliding backward, the other gliding backward the other way. But wait. They started at rest. Total momentum was zero. They end in motion, in opposite directions. Total momentum is still zero, because momentum is a vector and the two arrows cancel. Nothing about this is obvious. Where did the motion come from? It came from the push. But here is the deep fact underneath: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Skater A pushes on skater B. Skater B pushes back on skater A with the same force. Same force, same time, opposite directions. Newton's third law. Multiply force by time and you get impulse, which equals change in momentum. The two impulses are equal and opposite. So the two momentum changes are equal and opposite. The total is unchanged. Always. This is why momentum conservation is not a theorem about ice or about skaters. It is a statement that the universe keeps books. No matter how complicated the collision, no matter how many pieces fly off, the vector sum of all momenta before equals the vector sum after. Kinetic energy is not so lucky. In a perfectly elastic collision it survives. In an inelastic one it leaks into heat and deformation. But momentum never leaks. It is the most reliable accounting in physics.

header_title: The Clock That Ignores Amplitude
tagline: A pendulum's period depends only on its length
question_text: Why does a pendulum keep the same rhythm at every swing size?
audio_script: Watch a grandfather clock. The pendulum swings, back and forth, back and forth, at the same tempo, hour after hour. Here is what is strange. As the clock runs down, the swing gets smaller. The bob travels a shorter arc. Yet the period does not change. A small swing and a large swing take exactly the same time. Why? Look at the forces. The restoring force on the bob comes from gravity pulling it back toward the bottom. For small angles, that force is proportional to the displacement. Double the displacement, double the force. That linearity is what makes the motion simple harmonic, and what makes the period independent of how far the bob swings. It is called isochronism, and Galileo noticed it while watching a chandelier sway in a cathedral. He timed it against his own pulse. The period depends only on the length of the pendulum and on g. Not on the mass of the bob. Not on the amplitude, as long as the angle stays small. Shorten the string, and the clock runs fast. Move the clock to the Moon, where g is smaller, and it runs slow. This is why pendulum clocks must be adjusted for latitude: the Earth is not perfectly round, so g varies slightly from place to place. A pendulum one meter long has a period of about two seconds. Cut it to a quarter of a meter, and the period halves to one second. Everything about the motion scales, but the rhythm stays pure.

header_title: Counting Crests at a Pier
tagline: The wave equation is just bookkeeping
question_text: What actually makes v = λf true?
audio_script: Imagine you are standing on a pier, counting the crests that slap against a post. You count five crests in one second. So the frequency is five hertz. Now you notice the spacing between crests. Each crest is two meters behind the one in front. So the wavelength is two meters. In that one second, how far has the wave train moved? You counted five crests, each two meters apart. So the leading edge must have traveled ten meters. The speed is ten meters per second. That is the entire content of v equals lambda times f. It is not a law someone handed down from on high. It is bookkeeping. You counted crests, you measured spacing, you multiplied. The equation is what your counting already implied. Now the surprising consequence. The frequency is set by the source. If a boat bobs up and down twice a second, it launches two crests per second, forever. The speed is set by the medium. On deep water, waves travel fast; on shallow water, they slow down. So when a wave train moves from deep water into shallow water, the frequency cannot change, but the speed does. That means the wavelength must stretch or shrink to keep the product true. Move to deeper water, and crests spread apart. The wave has no choice. The universe enforces the accounting.

header_title: Blow Across a Sheet of Paper
tagline: It rises. You would have guessed it would sink.
question_text: Why does fast-moving air push less?
audio_script: Hold a sheet of paper by its edge and blow across the top. The paper lifts. Most people expect it to be pushed down, because you are blowing on it. It rises instead. Here is why. Moving air has lower pressure than still air at the same height. This is Bernoulli's principle, and it is one of the most counterintuitive facts in everyday physics. The reason is energy. A fluid element moving fast has more kinetic energy than one moving slowly. If nothing else is pushing energy into the fluid, then the pressure, which is a form of energy density, must drop to compensate. Pressure plus half rho v squared plus rho g h equals a constant along a streamline. Where the speed goes up, the pressure must go down. Watch this in a venturi tube. The pipe narrows, and by continuity the fluid must speed up to get through the tight section. But as the fluid speeds up, its pressure drops. You can see the pressure drop directly if you stick a vertical tube into the narrow section: the fluid rises less than it does in the wide section. Every atomizer, every carburetor, every chimney, every curveball, and every airplane wing leans on this same fact. The air on the curved top of a wing moves faster than the air underneath, so the pressure up there is lower, and the wing is pushed upward. Not because the wing is being sucked up, but because the ordinary pressure underneath has no counterweight above. Fast air, low pressure. Slow air, high pressure. It is that simple and that strange.

header_title: The Field Is the Messenger
tagline: How a charge knows another charge is nearby
question_text: How does one charge feel another without touching it?
audio_script: How does one charge know another charge is nearby? It cannot see. It cannot shout. Yet if you bring two positive charges close together, they repel, instantly, with no visible connection between them. Newton called this action at a distance, and he hated it. He thought it was the greatest absurdity in physics. Faraday found a way out. Instead of saying that one charge reaches across space and pulls on another, say that each charge creates something in the space around it. That something is the electric field. Picture a small positive test charge you can carry around. At every point in space, the field tells you what force that test charge would feel. Near a positive charge, the field arrows point outward, like porcupine quills. Farther away, they thin out. Double the distance, and each arrow gets four times weaker, because the field falls off as one over r squared. Now place a second charge in this field. It does not need to know that the first charge exists. It only feels the field at its own location, and responds locally. The first charge creates the field. The field travels. The second charge responds. Action at a distance becomes two local events, connected by a messenger. This is one of the great conceptual shifts in physics, and it is why the field concept survived from Faraday to Maxwell to Einstein. A charge never reaches across space. It only changes the space right around it.

header_title: Push Harder as You Go
tagline: Work is the area under the force curve
question_text: How do you add up a force that keeps changing?
audio_script: Imagine pushing a crate across a rough warehouse floor. At first, easy. As you go, the resistance grows, and you have to push harder. When you finally reach the far wall, you are tired. Where did your energy go? Into the crate, in the form of kinetic energy, and into friction, in the form of heat. But how much went into the crate? You cannot just multiply force by distance, because the force kept changing. Here is the trick. Break the whole journey into tiny steps, each so short that the force is essentially constant across it. On each tiny step, the work is force times step length: a little rectangle under the force curve. Add up all the rectangles, and you get the total work. Take the limit as the steps shrink to zero, and the sum becomes an integral. The work done by a variable force is the area under the force-versus-position curve. That is all calculus is: it is bookkeeping for things that change. And once you have the total work, the work-energy theorem tells you what it did. The net work on the object equals the change in its kinetic energy. Push with more net work than friction removes, and the object speeds up. Push with less, and it slows down. This is not a new law. It is Newton's second law, integrated over position, dressed up in energy language. But the phrasing is powerful, because energy bookkeeping ignores the messy details of the trajectory. You only need the beginning and the end.

header_title: Drop and Shoot Land Together
tagline: Horizontal motion does not help you fall
question_text: Which hits the ground first, a dropped ball or a fired one?
audio_script: Stand on a table with two identical balls. Hold one in each hand. Drop the left one straight down. At the same instant, fire the right one horizontally, as fast as you can. Which hits the floor first? Almost everyone says the fired one will take longer, because it has farther to travel. It does have farther to travel. But it does not take longer. Both hit the floor at the same instant. The reason is that horizontal motion and vertical motion do not talk to each other. Gravity pulls down. It has no opinion about horizontal speed. A ball moving at five meters per second sideways falls at exactly the same rate as one moving at fifty. The vertical fall is identical. It is as if the horizontal motion did not exist. This is Newton's second law, split into components. F x equals zero, so a x equals zero, so v x is constant. F y equals minus m g, so a y equals minus g, so the ball accelerates downward at exactly the same rate as a dropped ball. The two motions combine into a curve, but they are two separate stories. Once you see this, projectile problems become easy. Write the horizontal motion as a straight line. Write the vertical motion as free fall. Then stitch them together by eliminating time. You get the parabolic path, the range formula, the maximum height, all of it. And you get the punchline for free: horizontal motion never helps you fall faster. It only carries you farther while you do.

header_title: The Skater Who Sped Up Without Pushing
tagline: Angular momentum is conserved
question_text: Why does a skater spin faster when she pulls her arms in?
audio_script: A figure skater glides across the ice, arms stretched wide, spinning slowly. She pulls her arms in to her chest. She spins faster. She did not push against anything. She did not do any obvious work. Where did the extra spin come from? The answer is that she never gained any spin at all. She always had it. What changed was how it was distributed. Angular momentum, L, is the rotational analogue of linear momentum. It equals the moment of inertia I times the angular velocity omega. The moment of inertia depends on how far the mass is from the axis of rotation. Arms out, the mass is far, so I is large. Arms in, the mass is close, so I is small. If no external torque acts on her, L is conserved. So if I drops, omega must rise to keep the product the same. That is the entire trick. It is the same physics that makes a diver tuck to complete more somersaults, and that makes a cat right itself in midair. There is something deeply satisfying about this, because it does not require any new forces. It is just angular bookkeeping. The skater does do work when she pulls her arms in, because she is moving mass against the centrifugal tendency, and that work goes into rotational kinetic energy. She spins faster and with more energy than before, but the total angular momentum is exactly what it was. Nature insists on the balance. She just rearranged the terms.

header_title: Free Fall Doesn't Care About Mass
tagline: Both balls hit the ground together
question_text: A 5 kg ball is dropped. What is its acceleration?
audio_script: Drop a bowling ball and a tennis ball from the same height. Most people bet on the bowling ball. Here is the surprise. The only force on each is gravity, which equals m g. So the net force divided by the mass is m g over m, which is g. The mass cancels. The acceleration is nine point eight meters per second squared, whatever the ball weighs. Answer A.

header_title: Double the Radius and Wait Longer
tagline: Kepler's third law in one minute
question_text: If the orbital radius doubles, by what factor does the period change?
audio_script: Double the radius of an orbit. You might guess the period doubles. Kepler's third law says no. The square of the period grows as the cube of the radius, so T scales as r to the three halves. Double r, and T multiplies by two to the three halves, which is two root two, about two point eight. The outer orbit is not just longer to travel, it is also slower. Both effects compound. Answer C.

header_title: When Carts Stick and Move Together
tagline: A 2 kg cart hits a 4 kg cart. They stick.
question_text: A 2 kg cart at 3 m/s hits a stationary 4 kg cart. They stick. Final speed?
audio_script: A two kilogram cart moving at three meters per second hits a stationary four kilogram cart. They stick together. Momentum is conserved. Before: two times three equals six kilogram meters per second. After, the combined mass is six kilograms. So the final speed is six divided by six, one meter per second. Kinetic energy is not conserved; most of it went into deformation. Answer A.

header_title: Why Pendulums Keep Time
tagline: The period ignores mass and amplitude
question_text: A one meter pendulum swings. What is its period? (g=9.8)
audio_script: A pendulum one meter long. What is its period? The formula is T equals two pi times the square root of L over g. Plug in L equals one, g equals nine point eight. The square root of one over nine point eight is about zero point three two. Two pi times that is about two seconds. Notice: no mass, no amplitude. That is why pendulums are clocks. Answer C.

header_title: Count Crests to Find the Speed
tagline: Five crests per second, two meters apart
question_text: A wave has wavelength 2 m and frequency 5 Hz. Speed?
audio_script: Stand at a pier and count crests. Five hit per second. Each crest is two meters behind the one in front. In one second, five waves times two meters each means ten meters of wave train swept past. So the speed is ten meters per second. That is the whole of v equals lambda f. Answer D.

header_title: Faster Water, Lower Pressure
tagline: Blow across paper and it rises
question_text: Water in a horizontal pipe speeds up. Does the pressure rise or fall?
audio_script: Water flows through a horizontal pipe. At point one, pressure is two times ten to the fifth, and speed is two. At point two, pressure is one point five times ten to the fifth. What is the speed there? Bernoulli says the sum of pressure and kinetic energy density is constant. Solve for v two. The result is about ten point two meters per second, so the closest answer is C. Faster flow, lower pressure. Answer C.

header_title: The Field Falls as One Over r Squared
tagline: Double the distance, quarter the field
question_text: Find E at 0.50 m from a +2.0 microcoulomb charge
audio_script: A point charge of plus two microcoulombs. Find the electric field at half a meter. E equals k Q over r squared. k is nine times ten to the ninth, Q is two times ten to the minus sixth, r squared is zero point two five. Multiply and divide, and you get seven point two times ten to the fourth newtons per coulomb. Answer C. Double the distance, and the field drops by a factor of four.

header_title: Add Up the Area Under the Curve
tagline: Work is integral of force
question_text: A force 3x^2 N acts from 0 to 2 m. How much work?
audio_script: A force that grows as three x squared acts from zero to two meters. You cannot just multiply force by distance, because the force keeps changing. Integrate instead. The antiderivative of three x squared is x cubed. Evaluate at two, subtract the value at zero. You get eight joules. The work is the shaded area under the curve. Answer B.

header_title: 30 and 60 Give the Same Range
tagline: sin 2θ is symmetric around 45
question_text: A ball launches at 20 m/s at 30 degrees. Range? (g=9.8)
audio_script: Fire a ball at twenty meters per second, thirty degrees above horizontal. Range equals v zero squared sine two theta over g. Sine of sixty degrees is about zero point eight six six. Twenty squared is four hundred. Divide by nine point eight, and you get about thirty five meters. Answer B. Fire at sixty degrees and you get the same range, because sine of two theta is the same for thirty and sixty.

header_title: Why a Disk Beats a Hoop
tagline: Torque of 12 N·m on a solid disk
question_text: A 12 N·m torque acts on a 4 kg, 0.5 m disk. Find alpha
audio_script: A solid disk of mass four kilograms and radius half a meter. A torque of twelve newton meters. Moment of inertia of a disk is one half m r squared, which is zero point five. Angular acceleration is torque over I, twelve over zero point five, twenty four radians per second squared. Answer D. A hoop with the same mass would resist more, because all its mass sits farther from the axis.
